decks.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations — Part 1: Complex numbers and their algebra
goals: Explain why real numbers are not enough and define the imaginary unit
Write a complex number as $a + bi$ and read its real and imaginary parts
Use the cycle of powers of $i$
Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers
Use the conjugate and the equality of complex numbers

slides.heading: Complex Numbers, Part 1: Algebra of complex numbers
slides.body_md: Some equations have no real solution. What new numbers make them solvable?

visual.alt: Flow diagram of the number systems, each larger than the last: natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers and finally complex numbers.
visual.caption: Each new set of numbers solves equations the previous one could not.

slides.narration: Welcome. Every time mathematicians met an equation with no answer, they enlarged the numbers. Whole numbers became integers, then fractions, then all real numbers. One more step remains: an equation like x squared plus one equals zero has no real root. In this part you meet complex numbers and learn to add, multiply and divide them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write numbers as **$a + bi$** and name the parts
Add, subtract, multiply and **divide** complex numbers
Use the **conjugate** and equal complex numbers
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will define the imaginary unit, write numbers in the form a plus b i, and use the repeating cycle of its powers. You will add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers, using the conjugate for division. Finally you will solve for unknown parts when two complex numbers are equal. These appear as objective and short answer questions.

slides.heading: Why we need new numbers
slides.body_md: The graph of $y = x^2 + 1$ stays above the $x$-axis, so $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has **no real root**. We invent a number $i$ with $i^2 = -1$ so that it has roots $\pm i$.

visual.alt: The parabola y equal x squared plus 1, opening upward with its lowest point at (0, 1). It stays above the x-axis everywhere, so it never meets the axis: the equation x squared plus 1 equal 0 has no real root.
visual.caption: $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has no real root: the parabola never touches the $x$-axis.

slides.narration: Look at the parabola y equals x squared plus one. It never reaches the x axis, because x squared is never negative. So the equation x squared plus one equals zero has no real solution. We fix this by inventing a new number, called i, whose square is minus one. Then the equation has two roots, i and minus i.

slides.heading: The imaginary unit and the form a + bi
slides.body_md: $i^2 = -1$. A **complex number** is $z = a + bi$ with $a, b$ real: $a = \mathrm{Re}(z)$ is the real part and $b = \mathrm{Im}(z)$ the imaginary part.

visual.alt: Table of four complex numbers with their real and imaginary parts: 7 minus 5 i has real part 7 and imaginary part minus 5; minus 2 plus i has parts minus 2 and 1; 6 is real with imaginary part 0; minus 9 i is purely imaginary with real part 0.
visual.caption: $z = a + bi$: real part $a$, imaginary part $b$ (a real number, not $bi$).

slides.narration: A complex number is written a plus b i, where a and b are real numbers. The number a is the real part and b is the imaginary part. Note that the imaginary part is just b, without the letter i. A number with imaginary part zero is real, and one with real part zero is purely imaginary. Real numbers are special complex numbers.

slides.heading: Powers of i
slides.body_md: The powers of $i$ repeat every four steps: $i, -1, -i, 1$. Divide the exponent by $4$ and keep the remainder.

visual.alt: Table of the powers of i from 1 to 8: i, minus 1, minus i, 1, then the same four values again, so the powers repeat in a cycle of length four.
visual.caption: The cycle $i, -1, -i, 1$ repeats every four powers.

slides.narration: Start with i. Then i squared is minus one, i cubed is minus i, and i to the fourth is one. After that the pattern repeats: i to the fifth is i again. So to find a large power, divide the exponent by four and look at the remainder. A remainder of zero gives one, one gives i, two gives minus one, and three gives minus i.

slides.heading: Reading the remainder
slides.body_md: $i^{n} = i^{r}$ where $r$ is the remainder of $n$ divided by $4$. Negative powers work too: $i^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{i} = -i$.

visual.alt: Table showing i to the power n by the remainder of n on division by 4: remainder 0 gives 1, remainder 1 gives i, remainder 2 gives minus 1, remainder 3 gives minus i.
visual.caption: $i^{n} = i^{r}$ where $r$ is the remainder of $n$ on division by $4$.

slides.narration: Here is the rule as a table. For example, i to the power thirty-five: thirty-five leaves remainder three on division by four, so the value is i cubed, which is minus i. Negative exponents follow the same cycle. One over i is minus i, because multiplying top and bottom by i gives i over minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a power of i
slides.body_md: What is the value of i to the power thirty-five?
slides.narration: Divide thirty-five by four and use the remainder.

slides.heading: Adding and subtracting
slides.body_md: Add or subtract the real parts and the imaginary parts separately: $(a + bi) \pm (c + di) = (a \pm c) + (b \pm d)i$.

visual.alt: Table for z one equal 5 plus 2 i and z two equal 3 minus 6 i: the sum adds real and imaginary parts to give 8 minus 4 i; the difference subtracts them to give 2 plus 8 i.
visual.caption: $z_1 = 5 + 2i$, $z_2 = 3 - 6i$: add or subtract part by part.

slides.narration: Adding complex numbers is like collecting like terms. Add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together. With five plus two i and three minus six i, the sum is eight minus four i. For subtraction, subtract each part. Be careful with signs: subtracting minus six i adds six i, giving two plus eight i.

slides.heading: Multiplying
slides.body_md: Multiply like brackets and replace $i^2$ by $-1$: $(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$.

visual.alt: Table showing the product of 4 plus 3 i and 2 minus 5 i in three steps: expand into four terms, replace i squared by minus 1, and collect real and imaginary parts to get 23 minus 14 i.
visual.caption: Multiply like brackets in algebra, then use $i^2 = -1$.

slides.narration: To multiply, expand the brackets as usual. You get four terms. The term with i squared becomes minus one times its coefficient. In the table, four plus three i times two minus five i expands to eight, minus twenty i, plus six i, minus fifteen i squared. The last term becomes plus fifteen, and the answer is twenty-three minus fourteen i.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a product and a sum
slides.body_md: Simplify $(4 - i)(2 + 5i) + (3 + 2i)$ and write the answer as $a + bi$.

visual.alt: Table for the expression 4 minus i times 2 plus 5 i, plus 3 plus 2 i: the product is 13 plus 18 i and adding 3 plus 2 i gives 16 plus 20 i.
visual.caption: Product first, then the sum.

slides.narration: First expand the product. Four times two is eight, four times five i is twenty i, minus i times two is minus two i, and minus i times five i is minus five i squared, which is plus five. So the product is thirteen plus eighteen i. Now add three plus two i. The real parts give sixteen and the imaginary parts give twenty. The answer is sixteen plus twenty i.

slides.heading: Quick check: a product
slides.body_md: Multiply five minus two i by three plus four i.
slides.narration: Expand, then replace i squared by minus one. Do not drop that last term.

slides.heading: The conjugate
slides.body_md: The **conjugate** of $z = a + bi$ is $\bar z = a - bi$. Then $z + \bar z = 2a$ and $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2$ are both real.

visual.alt: Table of four complex numbers with their conjugates, sums and products: for 6 minus 5 i the conjugate is 6 plus 5 i, the sum is 12 and the product is 61; every sum and every product is a real number.
visual.caption: $z + \bar z = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(z)$ and $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2$ are always real.

math: \bar z = a - bi,\quad z\bar z = a^2 + b^2
slides.narration: The conjugate of a complex number keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part. The table shows four examples. In every row the sum of a number and its conjugate is real, and so is their product. The product equals the sum of the squares of the two parts, which is never negative. This product is the key to division.

slides.heading: Dividing: use the conjugate
slides.body_md: To divide, multiply top and bottom by the **conjugate of the divisor**. The denominator becomes the real number $c^2 + d^2$.

rows: Conjugate of the divisor: $c + di \to c - di$
Multiply the top and the bottom by it
Denominator: $(c + di)(c - di) = c^2 + d^2$, a real number
Expand the top, then split into real and imaginary parts

visual.alt: Table of the four steps of complex division: take the conjugate of the divisor, multiply top and bottom by it, note that the new denominator is the real number c squared plus d squared, then expand the numerator and split into real and imaginary parts.
visual.caption: Division is rationalising with the conjugate.

slides.narration: To divide by a complex number, multiply top and bottom by its conjugate. The new denominator is real, because a number times its conjugate is the sum of two squares. Here we divide seven plus four i by three minus two i. The numerator becomes thirteen plus twenty-six i, the denominator is thirteen, and the quotient is one plus two i. Check by multiplying back.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a quotient
slides.body_md: Express $\dfrac{7 + 4i}{3 - 2i}$ in the form $a + bi$.

visual.alt: Table dividing 7 plus 4 i by 3 minus 2 i: multiply top and bottom by 3 plus 2 i, the numerator becomes 13 plus 26 i, the denominator becomes 13, the quotient is 1 plus 2 i and multiplying back gives 7 plus 4 i.
visual.caption: Rationalise the denominator with the conjugate.

slides.narration: We multiply top and bottom by three plus two i. The numerator expands to twenty-one plus fourteen i plus twelve i plus eight i squared, which is thirteen plus twenty-six i. The denominator is nine plus four, which is thirteen. Dividing each part by thirteen gives one plus two i. To be safe, multiply one plus two i by three minus two i and confirm you get seven plus four i.

slides.heading: Quick check: a high power
slides.body_md: Evaluate one minus i to the power eight.
slides.narration: Square it first and see what you get.

slides.heading: Equal complex numbers
slides.body_md: Two complex numbers are equal when their **real parts are equal** and their **imaginary parts are equal**.

visual.alt: Table of the equality rule for complex numbers: two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal, with two examples.
visual.caption: Compare parts, never the whole numbers.

slides.narration: One complex equation gives two real equations. If a plus i b equals c plus i d, then a equals c and b equals d. So an equation with two unknown real numbers can be solved by comparing the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. This is the standard way to find unknown letters in complex number problems.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: find x and y
slides.body_md: Find real $x$ and $y$ if $(2x - y) + i(x + 3y) = 3 + 5i$.

visual.alt: Table solving the equation 2x minus y plus i times x plus 3y equal 3 plus 5 i: equate real parts and imaginary parts to get two linear equations, solve to find x equal 2 and y equal 1, and check.
visual.caption: $a + ib = c + id \iff a = c$ and $b = d$.

slides.narration: Compare real parts: two x minus y equals three. Compare imaginary parts: x plus three y equals five. From the first, y equals two x minus three. Substitute into the second to get seven x minus nine equals five, so x is two and y is one. Check by substituting back: both sides become three plus five i.

slides.heading: Quick check: a true or false
slides.body_md: True or false: the product of two non-real complex numbers can be real.
slides.narration: Try a number and its conjugate.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $i^2 = -1$; powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of four
Add and subtract part by part; multiply like brackets
$\bar z = a - bi$; $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2$
Divide using the conjugate of the divisor; equal numbers have equal parts

nodes.label: Divide with the conjugate; equal parts

visual.alt: Summary flow: the imaginary unit squares to minus 1 and its powers repeat; complex numbers add, subtract and multiply like brackets; the conjugate makes a product real; division uses the conjugate and equality compares parts.
visual.caption: Algebra of complex numbers in four steps.

slides.narration: To sum up. The imaginary unit squares to minus one and its powers cycle with period four. Complex numbers add and subtract part by part and multiply like brackets. The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part, and a number times its conjugate is real, which is how we divide. Two complex numbers are equal when both their parts match.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Equal numbers (1–2 marks):** two equations, two values
**Product or quotient (2–3 marks):** expansion, conjugate step, final $a + bi$
**Powers of $i$ (1–2 marks):** remainder on division by $4$
**Mistake:** writing the imaginary part as $bi$ instead of $b$
slides.narration: In product and quotient questions, marks go for the expansion, for using the conjugate of the divisor, and for the final answer in the form a plus b i. In equality questions you earn a mark for each equation. Watch for three slips: forgetting that i squared is minus one, calling the imaginary part b i instead of b, and dividing without multiplying by the conjugate.

decks.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations — Part 2: Argand plane, modulus, polar form and quadratic equations
goals: Represent complex numbers on the Argand plane
Find the modulus and the conjugate and use their properties
Interpret the conjugate and the sum geometrically
Write a complex number in polar form (formative)
Solve quadratics with real coefficients and complex roots (formative)

slides.heading: Complex Numbers, Part 2: The Argand plane
slides.body_md: Every complex number is a point of a plane. What does its size and direction tell us?

series.label: arrow from the origin to the point 1
arrow from the origin to the point 2
arrow from the origin to the point 3
arrow from the origin to the point 4

visual.alt: The Argand plane with four points, one in each quadrant: 3 plus 2 i in the first, minus 2 plus 3 i in the second, minus 3 minus i in the third and 2 minus 3 i in the fourth, each joined to the origin. The real part is read along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part along the vertical axis.
visual.caption: Each $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$: real part across, imaginary part up.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A complex number a plus b i can be drawn as the point a comma b, with the real part across and the imaginary part up. This is the Argand plane. In this part you will read distance and direction from the picture, meet the modulus and conjugate as geometric ideas, and see how complex numbers connect to quadratic equations.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Plot complex numbers on the **Argand plane**
Find the **modulus** and **conjugate** and use their rules
See the **conjugate** as a mirror image and the sum as a parallelogram
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will plot complex numbers and find their modulus and conjugate. You will use the rules for the modulus of products and quotients, and see the conjugate and the sum as pictures. The polar form and quadratic equations with complex roots are formative topics: they are taught for understanding and are not assessed in the annual board paper.

slides.heading: The Argand plane
slides.body_md: $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$: **real axis** across, **imaginary axis** up. The sign pair tells the quadrant.

series.label: arrow from the origin to the point 1
arrow from the origin to the point 2
arrow from the origin to the point 3
arrow from the origin to the point 4

visual.alt: The Argand plane with four points, one in each quadrant: 3 plus 2 i in the first, minus 2 plus 3 i in the second, minus 3 minus i in the third and 2 minus 3 i in the fourth, each joined to the origin. The real part is read along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part along the vertical axis.
visual.caption: Each $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$: real part across, imaginary part up.

slides.narration: In the Argand plane the horizontal axis holds the real part and the vertical axis holds the imaginary part. The number three plus two i is three across and two up, in the first quadrant. Minus two plus three i is in the second quadrant, minus three minus i is in the third, and two minus three i is in the fourth. Real numbers lie on the horizontal axis.

slides.heading: Quick check: which quadrant?
slides.body_md: In which quadrant does the reciprocal of minus two plus i lie?
slides.narration: Rationalise first, then read the signs of the two parts.

slides.heading: The conjugate as a mirror image
slides.body_md: $\bar z$ is the reflection of $z$ in the **real axis**: same real part, opposite imaginary part. $z$ and $\bar z$ are equally far from the origin.

series.label: arrow from the origin to z
arrow from the origin to the conjugate
segment joining z and its conjugate

visual.alt: The Argand plane with the point z equal 4 plus 3 i above the real axis and its conjugate 4 minus 3 i directly below it. The two points are mirror images in the horizontal real axis and are equally far from the origin.
visual.caption: The conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis.

slides.narration: On the Argand plane the conjugate of a number is its mirror image in the real axis. Four plus three i sits three units above the axis, and its conjugate four minus three i sits three units below it. The two points are the same distance from the origin. This picture explains why a number and its conjugate have the same modulus.

slides.heading: The modulus
slides.body_md: $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is the distance of $z = a + bi$ from the origin. $|z| = 5$ describes a **circle** about the origin.

series.label: radius to 3 + 4i, of length 5

visual.alt: The Argand plane with the circle of radius 5 about the origin. Six marked points lie on it: 3 plus 4 i, minus 3 plus 4 i, minus 4 minus 3 i, 4 minus 3 i, 5 i and minus 5 i. The radius to 3 plus 4 i has length 5.
visual.caption: All points with $|z| = 5$ lie on one circle about the origin.

slides.narration: The modulus of a complex number is its distance from the origin, found with the Pythagorean theorem. The number three plus four i has modulus the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five. Every point at distance five from the origin lies on one circle. So the equation modulus of z equals five describes a circle with centre at the origin and radius five.

slides.heading: Rules for the modulus

visual.alt: Table checking four modulus rules for z one equal 2 plus i and z two equal 3 minus 2 i: the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli, the modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli, a number and its conjugate have the same modulus, and z times its conjugate equals the modulus squared.
visual.caption: $z_1 = 2 + i$, $z_2 = 3 - 2i$.

slides.narration: The modulus behaves well with products and quotients: the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli, and the modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli. A number and its conjugate have the same modulus, and a number times its conjugate equals the modulus squared. The table checks each rule for two and three specific numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: modulus of a product
slides.body_md: Find $|(2 + i)(3 - 2i)|$ in two ways.

visual.alt: Table finding the modulus of the product of 2 plus i and 3 minus 2 i two ways: the product is 8 minus i with modulus root 65, and the rule gives root 5 times root 13, which is also root 65.
visual.caption: Both routes agree.

slides.narration: Method one: multiply out. Two plus i times three minus two i gives eight minus i. Its modulus is the square root of sixty-four plus one, which is the square root of sixty-five. Method two: use the rule. The modulus of two plus i is root five, and the modulus of three minus two i is root thirteen. Their product is root sixty-five. The two methods agree, and the rule is much quicker for long products.

slides.heading: Quick check: a distance
slides.body_md: How far from the origin is the point nine minus twelve i?
slides.narration: Use the square root of the sum of squares.

slides.heading: Addition as a parallelogram
slides.body_md: $z_1 + z_2$ is the fourth corner of the parallelogram on $0$, $z_1$ and $z_2$. Hence $|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|$ (the **triangle inequality**).

series.label: arrow from the origin to z one
arrow from the origin to z two
arrow from the origin to the sum
side parallel to z two
side parallel to z one

visual.alt: The Argand plane with z one equal 2 plus 3 i, z two equal 3 minus i and their sum 5 plus 2 i. The origin, z one, the sum and z two are the corners of a parallelogram, and the diagonal from the origin is the sum.
visual.caption: $z_1 + z_2$ is the fourth corner of the parallelogram on $z_1$ and $z_2$.

slides.narration: To add complex numbers on the plane, complete the parallelogram. Two plus three i and three minus i have the sum five plus two i, the fourth corner. The diagonal from the origin is shorter than the two sides together, which is the triangle inequality: the modulus of a sum is at most the sum of the moduli. Equality holds only when the two numbers point in the same direction.

slides.heading: Polar form (formative only)
slides.body_md: $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta$ the **argument**, the angle from the positive real axis. *Taught for understanding; not assessed in the annual paper.*

visual.alt: Axes with the point z equal 1 plus root 3 i in the first quadrant. The segment from the origin to z has length 2 and makes an angle of 60 degrees with the positive real axis; a dashed perpendicular goes down to the real axis.
visual.caption: $z = 1 + \sqrt{3}\,i$: modulus $2$, argument $60^\circ$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: A point can be described by its distance from the origin and its direction. The distance is the modulus r. The direction is the argument, the angle theta that the line to the point makes with the positive real axis. For one plus root three i, the modulus is two and the angle is sixty degrees. The polar form is r times cosine theta plus i sine theta. This topic is for understanding and is not assessed in the annual paper.

slides.heading: The argument by position
slides.body_md: The **principal argument** lies in $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$. Use the quadrant: find the related angle $\alpha$ with $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|b|}{|a|}$, then place it.

visual.alt: Table of principal arguments: 1 plus i has 45 degrees, minus 1 plus i has 135, minus 1 minus i has minus 135, 1 minus i has minus 45; the positive real axis has 0, the positive imaginary axis 90, the negative real axis 180 and the negative imaginary axis minus 90 degrees.
visual.caption: The principal argument lies in $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$, measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis.

slides.narration: The principal argument is measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis and lies between minus one hundred eighty and one hundred eighty degrees. First find the related acute angle using the tangent of the absolute values. Then adjust for the quadrant. Points on the axes have the arguments zero, ninety, one hundred eighty and minus ninety degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a polar form
slides.body_md: Write $-1 - \sqrt{3}\,i$ in polar form.

visual.alt: Table converting minus 1 minus root 3 i to polar form: modulus 2, third quadrant, related angle 60 degrees, principal argument minus 120 degrees, so 2 times cosine of minus 120 degrees plus i sine of minus 120 degrees.
visual.caption: $z = -1 - \sqrt{3}\,i$.

slides.narration: First the modulus: the square root of one plus three is two. Both parts are negative, so the point is in the third quadrant. The tangent of the related angle is root three, so the related angle is sixty degrees. In the third quadrant the principal argument is minus one hundred eighty plus sixty, which is minus one hundred twenty degrees. The polar form follows.

slides.heading: Quick check: an argument
slides.body_md: True or false: the principal argument of minus four i is minus ninety degrees.
slides.narration: Which axis is minus four i on?

slides.heading: Quadratic equations with complex roots (formative only)
slides.body_md: If $b^2 - 4ac < 0$ (real $a, b, c$), then $x = \dfrac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}$: two **non-real roots, conjugate** to each other.

visual.alt: Table of three quadratic equations with negative discriminants and their complex roots: x squared plus 4 equal 0 has roots plus and minus 2 i; x squared plus 2 x plus 5 has roots minus 1 plus or minus 2 i; x squared minus 6 x plus 10 has roots 3 plus or minus i.
visual.caption: Each root pair is a conjugate pair.

slides.narration: The quadratic formula now works for every real quadratic. When the discriminant is negative, its square root is i times a real number, so the two roots are non-real. They are conjugates of each other. The table shows three equations with negative discriminants. Solving quadratics over complex numbers is a formative topic and is not assessed in the annual paper.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: solving a quadratic
slides.body_md: Solve $x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0$ and check one root.

visual.alt: Table solving x squared plus 2 x plus 5 equal 0: the discriminant is minus 16, the roots are minus 1 plus or minus 2 i, and substituting minus 1 plus 2 i gives zero.
visual.caption: $x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0$.

slides.narration: The discriminant is four minus twenty, which is minus sixteen, so the roots are not real. The square root of minus sixteen is four i. The roots are minus two plus or minus four i, all over two, giving minus one plus or minus two i. To check, square minus one plus two i to get minus three minus four i, add minus two plus four i, and add five. The total is zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: modulus of a root
slides.body_md: Find the common modulus of the two roots of x squared minus ten x plus one hundred sixty-nine.
slides.narration: Solve the quadratic first, then take the modulus.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$ of the Argand plane
$|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; $\bar z$ is the mirror image in the real axis
Negative discriminant: a conjugate pair of non-real roots (formative)

visual.alt: Summary flow: complex numbers are points of the Argand plane; the modulus is the distance from the origin and the conjugate is the mirror image; the polar form uses modulus and argument; a quadratic with negative discriminant has a conjugate pair of roots.
visual.caption: Argand plane, modulus, polar form and quadratics.

slides.narration: To sum up. Complex numbers are points of the Argand plane. The modulus is the distance from the origin and the conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli. The polar form uses the modulus and the argument. And a real quadratic with a negative discriminant has two conjugate roots that are not real.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Modulus and conjugate (1–2 marks):** formula, exact surd, correct sign
**Argand plane (1–2 marks):** correct quadrant from the signs
**Property verification (3 marks):** both sides computed separately
**Mistake:** $|a + bi| = a + b$ instead of $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$
**Mistake:** giving the related angle instead of the argument
**Light topics:** polar form and complex quadratics are formative only
slides.narration: For modulus questions, write the formula, keep the answer as an exact square root, and mind the signs. For the Argand plane, read the quadrant from the signs of the two parts. In verification questions compute both sides separately. Avoid three slips: adding a and b instead of using squares, giving the related angle instead of the argument, and spending long on polar form and complex quadratics, which are formative only.

notes.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Need for complex numbers; the imaginary unit
sections.body_md:
The equation $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has no real root because $x^2 \ge 0$. We introduce the **imaginary unit** $i$ with $i^2 = -1$.

A **complex number** is $z = a + bi$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: $a = \mathrm{Re}(z)$, $b = \mathrm{Im}(z)$. If $b = 0$ it is real; if $a = 0$ and $b \ne 0$ it is purely imaginary. Every real number is complex.

**Powers of $i$:** $i, -1, -i, 1$ repeat in a cycle of four, so $i^{n} = i^{r}$ where $r$ is the remainder of $n$ on division by $4$ (also for negative $n$: $i^{-1} = -i$). Any four consecutive powers add to $0$.

key_terms.definition_md: A number $a + bi$ with $a, b$ real.
$a$ and $b$ (the imaginary part is the real number $b$, not $bi$).

visual.alt: The parabola y equal x squared plus 1, opening upward with its lowest point at (0, 1). It stays above the x-axis everywhere, so it never meets the axis: the equation x squared plus 1 equal 0 has no real root.
visual.caption: $x^2 + 1 = 0$ has no real root: the parabola never touches the $x$-axis.

sections.heading: 2. Equality, addition, subtraction and multiplication
sections.body_md:
**Equality:** $a + bi = c + di \iff a = c$ and $b = d$. One complex equation gives two real equations.

**Sum and difference:** $(a + bi) \pm (c + di) = (a \pm c) + (b \pm d)i$.

**Product:** expand and use $i^2 = -1$: $(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i$.

Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, and multiplication distributes over addition, exactly as for real numbers. There is **no ordering** of complex numbers: $2 + 3i > 1 + 2i$ has no meaning.

sections.heading: 3. Conjugate, reciprocal and division
sections.body_md:
The **conjugate** of $z = a + bi$ is $\bar z = a - bi$.

- $z + \bar z = 2a$ (real) and $z - \bar z = 2bi$ (purely imaginary).
- $z\bar z = a^2 + b^2$ (real, non-negative).
- $\bar{\bar z} = z$; $z$ is real iff $\bar z = z$.

**Reciprocal:** $\dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{\bar z}{a^2 + b^2}$ for $z \ne 0$.

**Division:** multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the divisor: $\dfrac{a + bi}{c + di} = \dfrac{(a + bi)(c - di)}{c^2 + d^2}$. Check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.

sections.heading: 4. The Argand plane
sections.body_md:
The complex number $a + bi$ is the point $(a, b)$: the **real axis** is horizontal and the **imaginary axis** vertical. Real numbers lie on the real axis and purely imaginary numbers on the imaginary axis.

The sign pair $(\mathrm{Re}, \mathrm{Im})$ gives the quadrant: $(+, +)$ first, $(-, +)$ second, $(-, -)$ third, $(+, -)$ fourth.

The conjugate $\bar z$ is the mirror image of $z$ in the real axis; $-z$ is the image in the origin; the sum $z_1 + z_2$ is the fourth corner of the parallelogram on $0, z_1, z_2$.

sections.heading: 5. The modulus and its properties
sections.body_md:
The **modulus** of $z = a + bi$ is $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the distance from the origin; keep exact surds.

- $|z| \ge 0$, and $|z| = 0$ only for $z = 0$.
- $|z_1 z_2| = |z_1||z_2|$ and $\left|\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right| = \dfrac{|z_1|}{|z_2|}$.
- $|\bar z| = |z|$ and $z\bar z = |z|^2$.
- $|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|$ (triangle inequality).

$|z| = k$ is the circle with centre at the origin and radius $k$. The moduli of complex numbers can be compared; the numbers themselves cannot.

sections.heading: 6. Polar form and argument (formative)
sections.body_md:
*Formative only: not assessed in the annual paper.*

Write $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta$ the **argument**, the angle from the positive real axis to the line from the origin to $z$ (anticlockwise positive). The **principal argument** lies in $(-180^\circ, 180^\circ]$.

To find $\theta$: take the related angle $\alpha$ with $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{|b|}{|a|}$ and place it using the quadrant. Examples: $1 + i$ has $\theta = 45^\circ$; $-1 - i$ has $-135^\circ$; $-4$ has $180^\circ$; $-4i$ has $-90^\circ$.

Check a polar form by expanding: $r\cos\theta = a$ and $r\sin\theta = b$.

sections.heading: 7. Quadratic equations with complex roots (formative)
sections.body_md:
*Formative only: not assessed in the annual paper.*

For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with real coefficients and discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$:

- $D > 0$: two distinct real roots; $D = 0$: equal real roots;
- $D < 0$: two **non-real roots** $\dfrac{-b \pm i\sqrt{-D}}{2a}$, which are **conjugates** of each other.

The sum of the roots is $-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and the product is $\dfrac{c}{a}$. For a conjugate pair the product equals the square of the common modulus. A real quadratic never has exactly one non-real root.

Check a root by substitution.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Equal complex numbers (1–2 marks):* two real equations, then $x$ and $y$.
- *Product or quotient (2–3 marks):* expansion, conjugate of the divisor, final $a + bi$.
- *Powers of $i$ (1–2 marks):* reduce the exponent modulo $4$.
- *Modulus and conjugate (1–2 marks):* formula, exact surd, correct signs.
- *Verification of a property (3 marks):* each side computed separately.
- *Argand plane (1–2 marks):* point, quadrant or mirror image.

**Common mistakes**
1. Forgetting $i^2 = -1$ when multiplying.
2. Writing the imaginary part as $bi$ instead of $b$.
3. Dividing without multiplying by the conjugate of the divisor.
4. $|a + bi| = a + b$ instead of $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
5. $\sqrt{-a}\sqrt{-b} = \sqrt{ab}$: the rule needs non-negative $a$ and $b$.
6. Treating $2 + 3i > 1 + 2i$ as meaningful: complex numbers are not ordered.
7. Giving the related angle as the argument.
8. Polar form and complex quadratics are formative only: do not over-invest.

questions.stem_md: The imaginary part of the complex number $7 - 5i$ is
questions.solution_md: Write $7 - 5i = 7 + (-5)i$. The imaginary part is the real coefficient of $i$, that is $-5$, without the letter $i$ and with its sign.

questions.stem_md: In the complex numbers, the power $i^{58}$ has the value
questions.solution_md: The powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of length four. Since $58 = 4 \times 14 + 2$, $i^{58} = i^{2} = -1$. Reading the remainder as $0$ would give $1$.

questions.stem_md: For every integer $n$, the sum $i^{n} + i^{n+1} + i^{n+2} + i^{n+3}$ equals
questions.solution_md: Factor out $i^{n}$: the sum is $i^{n}(1 + i + i^2 + i^3) = i^{n}(1 + i - 1 - i) = 0$. So four consecutive powers always cancel.

questions.stem_md: Collecting real parts and imaginary parts separately, $(6 - 2i) + (-4 + 9i) - (3 + i)$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: Real parts: $6 - 4 - 3 = -1$. Imaginary parts: $-2 + 9 - 1 = 6$. So the result is $-1 + 6i$. Forgetting to change both signs of $3 + i$ gives $5 + 8i$ or $-1 + 8i$.

questions.stem_md: The product $(5 - 2i)(3 + 4i)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $(5 - 2i)(3 + 4i) = 15 + 20i - 6i - 8i^2 = 15 + 14i + 8 = 23 + 14i$. Dropping the $i^2$ term, or giving it the wrong sign, leads to $15 + 14i$, $7 + 14i$ or $23 + 26i$.

questions.stem_md: If $z = 4 + 3i$, the conjugate of $z^2$ is
questions.solution_md: $z^2 = 16 + 24i + 9i^2 = 7 + 24i$, and changing the sign of the imaginary part gives $\overline{z^2} = 7 - 24i$. The same value comes from $(\bar z)^2 = (4 - 3i)^2$. Option (c) forgets $i^2 = -1$.

questions.stem_md: The multiplicative inverse of the complex number $5 + 12i$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiply top and bottom of $\dfrac{1}{5 + 12i}$ by the conjugate $5 - 12i$: the denominator becomes $25 + 144 = 169$, so the inverse is $\dfrac{5 - 12i}{169}$. Dividing by $13$ instead of $169$ uses the modulus instead of its square.

questions.stem_md: Rationalising the denominator, $\dfrac{2 + 9i}{1 - 2i}$ becomes
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{1 + 2i}{1 + 2i}$: the numerator is $(2 + 9i)(1 + 2i) = 2 + 4i + 9i - 18 = -16 + 13i$ and the denominator is $1 + 4 = 5$. So the quotient is $\dfrac{-16 + 13i}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: Real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy $(x + 2y) + i(3x - y) = 7 - 7i$. The value of $x + y$ is
questions.solution_md: Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts: $x + 2y = 7$ and $3x - y = -7$. Then $y = 3x + 7$, so $7x + 14 = 7$, giving $x = -1$ and $y = 4$. Hence $x + y = 3$.

questions.stem_md: The complex number $z$ satisfies $z + 3\bar z = 8 + 4i$. Then $z$ equals
questions.solution_md: Let $z = a + bi$, so $\bar z = a - bi$ and $z + 3\bar z = 4a - 2bi$. Comparing with $8 + 4i$: $4a = 8$ gives $a = 2$ and $-2b = 4$ gives $b = -2$. So $z = 2 - 2i$.

questions.stem_md: How far from the origin of the Argand plane does the point representing $-4 - 9i$ lie?
questions.solution_md: The distance is the modulus $|-4 - 9i| = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-9)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 81} = \sqrt{97}$. Option (d) adds the two coordinates and (a) forgets the square root.

questions.stem_md: Let $w = \dfrac{(1 + i)(2 - i)}{1 - 2i}$. The modulus $|w|$ equals
questions.solution_md: Use $\left|\dfrac{z_1 z_2}{z_3}\right| = \dfrac{|z_1||z_2|}{|z_3|} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{2}$. Option (a) is $|w|^2$, and (b) forgets to divide by $|1 - 2i|$.

questions.stem_md: The point representing $\dfrac{1}{-2 + i}$ on the Argand plane lies in the
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{-2 + i} = \dfrac{-2 - i}{(-2)^2 + 1^2} = \dfrac{-2 - i}{5}$. Both the real part $-\dfrac{2}{5}$ and the imaginary part $-\dfrac{1}{5}$ are negative: third quadrant. Taking the position of $-2 + i$ itself gives the second quadrant.

questions.stem_md: The roots of the quadratic equation $x^2 + 2x + 10 = 0$ are
questions.solution_md: The discriminant is $2^2 - 4(1)(10) = -36$, so $x = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{-36}}{2} = \dfrac{-2 \pm 6i}{2} = -1 \pm 3i$. Skipping the division by $2a$ gives $-2 \pm 6i$.

questions.stem_md: The real numbers $p$ and $q$ are such that $2 + 3i$ is a root of $x^2 + px + q = 0$. Then $(p, q)$ is
questions.solution_md: The coefficients are real, so the other root is the conjugate $2 - 3i$. Sum of roots $= 4 = -p$, so $p = -4$; product $= (2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 4 + 9 = 13 = q$.

questions.stem_md: For a complex number $z$, the product $z\,\bar z$ is the same as
questions.solution_md: With $z = a + bi$: $z\bar z = (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - b^2 i^2 = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2$. For $z = 3 + 4i$ the product is $25$, while $|z| = 5$ and $z^2 = -7 + 24i$.

questions.stem_md: The product of two non-real complex numbers can be a real number.
questions.solution_md: For example $i \times i = -1$ and $(2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 13$: each factor is non-real but the product is real.

questions.stem_md: The power $i^{100}$ equals $-1$.
questions.solution_md: $100 = 4 \times 25$, so $i^{100} = (i^4)^{25} = 1^{25} = 1$, not $-1$. The value $-1$ would belong to an exponent leaving remainder $2$ on division by $4$.

questions.stem_md: In the complex numbers, the inequality $2 + 3i > 1 + 2i$ is a meaningful statement that is true.
questions.solution_md: Non-real complex numbers cannot be ordered: there is no consistent meaning of "greater than" for them, so the inequality has no meaning. Only their moduli (real numbers) can be compared, e.g. $|2 + 3i| = \sqrt{13}$ and $|1 + 2i| = \sqrt{5}$.

questions.stem_md: The principal argument of the purely imaginary number $-4i$ is $-90^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: The point $(0, -4)$ is on the negative imaginary axis, a quarter-turn clockwise from the positive real axis, so its principal argument is $-90^\circ$.

Find the real number $k$ for which $\dfrac{k + 3i}{2 - i}$ is a real number.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{k + 3i}{2 - i} = \dfrac{(k + 3i)(2 + i)}{5} = \dfrac{(2k - 3) + (k + 6)i}{5}$. It is real when the imaginary part vanishes: $k + 6 = 0$, so $k = -6$.

questions.stem_md: Find the positive real number $a$ for which the point $a - 2i$ lies at distance $2\sqrt{10}$ from the origin of the Argand plane.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $i = i$, $i^2 = -1$, $i^3 = i^2 \cdot i = -i$, $i^4 = (i^2)^2 = 1$. The cycle has length $4$.

**(b)** $83 = 4 \times 20 + 3$, so $i^{83} = i^3 = -i$. For the negative power, $i^{-26} = \dfrac{1}{i^{26}}$ and $26 = 4 \times 6 + 2$ gives $i^{26} = -1$, so $i^{-26} = -1$.

**(d)** $(1 + i)^2 = 2i$, so $(1 + i)^{10} = (2i)^5 = 32\,i^5 = 32i^{4} \cdot i = 32i$.

Consider the equation $2x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0$.

(a) Find its discriminant and say what kind of roots it has.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $D = (-6)^2 - 4(2)(5) = 36 - 40 = -4$. It is negative, so the roots are non-real and conjugate.

**(b)** $x = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{-4}}{4} = \dfrac{6 \pm 2i}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2} \pm \dfrac{1}{2}i$, i.e. $x = \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}i$ or $x = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}i$.

**(c)** Sum $= \left(\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}i\right) + \left(\dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}i\right) = 3$. Product $= \dfrac{9}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4}i^2 = \dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, that is $\dfrac{5}{2}$.

**(d)** For each root $|x|^2 = \dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, so both roots are at distance $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2}$ from the origin. This is $\sqrt{c/a}$ for the equation.
